sections.text:
The same sad story is told again and again. Israel turns to other gods. An enemy takes the land. The people groan, and the LORD raises up a savior. The first of them is Othniel, and others follow: Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson are the best known. But each time the judge dies, the people go back and deal “more corruptly than their fathers”.

So the cycle does not go round. It spirals downward. By the last chapters, 17 to 21, the book has reached some of the darkest pages in the Bible.

Then it closes on one plain sentence that explains the whole book: “In those days there was no king in Israel.” Everyone did what seemed right to them. Between Joshua and the first kings, the people had no one to hold them together, and the book shows what that cost.

The judges were tribal leaders and deliverers, more than judges in a courtroom. The period is commonly placed between about 1200 and 1050 before Christ, after the days of Joshua and before the first kings. At this time Israel was a loose group of tribes without a central government.

Most readers take the book as a description of what happened, not as a recommendation. The violence, including terrible violence against women, is told as evidence of how far the people had fallen, and the telling does not praise it.

Yet Hebrews 11 still names several of the judges as examples of faith. Many readers see in that a sign that God works through deeply flawed people. The book leaves its reader looking for a better leader than any it describes.

Joshua is dead, and the people ask the LORD who should go up first. The answer is Judah. Judah asks his brother Simeon to join him, and together they win at Bezek. They catch the king there, Adoni-Bezek, and cut off his thumbs and big toes. He says, in the text’s own words, that seventy kings had scavenged under his table, and that as he had done, God had done to him.

The chapter then offers a bright list: Jerusalem struck, Hebron given to Caleb, Othniel winning Achsah as his wife, and the LORD was with Judah. After that comes a different tone. “he could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron.”

Tribe after tribe follows: Benjamin, Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali. Each “didn’t drive out” the people of the land. The Danites are pushed into the hills.

Judges takes up the story after Joshua. The first chapter repeats some events from the book of Joshua, with Caleb and Othniel; see Joshua 15. It sets the mood for the whole book: promising beginnings followed by incomplete results. Scholars debate how the account fits with Joshua’s picture of a nearly complete conquest. The cruel treatment of Adoni-Bezek is told without comment on whether it was right. Judges 2 explains what the writer thinks this means.

An angel of the LORD comes up from Gilgal to a place called Bochim and speaks to all of Israel. The LORD brought them out of Egypt and into this land and promised never to break the covenant. They were told not to make covenants with the people here, and they did. “Why have you done this?” Then the people lift up their voices and weep. They name the place Bochim, which the text connects with weeping.

The story then steps back and sketches a pattern. Joshua dies. Another generation rises, one that does not know the LORD. They serve the Baals, and the LORD gives them to raiders. In their distress the LORD raises up judges to save them. But when each judge dies, the people turn back, “more corruptly than their fathers”.

So the LORD says he will no longer drive out the nations Joshua left, and will use them to test Israel.

This chapter is the key to the book. It explains why the stories that follow repeat: sin, oppression, a cry for help, a rescuer, a time of rest, and then a new fall. Scholars often point out that the cycle shows Israel moving downhill. Baal was the storm god of Canaan, and Ashtaroth were goddesses linked to him. The first verses of the chapter echo the covenant warnings in Deuteronomy 7 and the end of Joshua 23.

The first verses ask why enemies were left in the land: to test Israel and to teach war to a new generation. Then the pattern begins. Israel marries among the peoples around them and serves their gods, and a king from Mesopotamia rules them for eight years. When they cry out, the LORD raises up Othniel, Caleb’s younger brother, and the land has rest for forty years.

Israel falls again, and Eglon of Moab holds them for eighteen. This time the rescuer is Ehud, a left-handed man from Benjamin. He carries tribute to the king, with a double-edged sword strapped under his clothing on his right thigh. Alone with Eglon in a cool upper room, he says, “I have a message from God to you.” Then he kills him. He locks the doors behind him and escapes.

Ehud blows a trumpet in the hills and leads Israel against Moab. The land rests eighty years. A line about Shamgar and an ox goad closes the chapter.

Othniel and Ehud are the first two judges. In this book a judge is a leader who rescues the people, not just a courtroom officer. Othniel is the connection with Joshua and Caleb; see Joshua 15. The story of Ehud is told with dark humor and many details, and readers have long found it striking. It is a story about violence, and the text does not offer a moral verdict on every act. The next judge, Deborah, comes in chapter 4.

For twenty years the Canaanite king Jabin, with a captain named Sisera and nine hundred chariots of iron, has pressed hard on Israel. The people cry to the LORD, and the chapter turns to a woman sitting under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel. Deborah is a prophetess, and Israel comes to her for judgment.

She sends for Barak and passes on the LORD’s command to lead ten thousand men to Mount Tabor. Barak says he will go only if she goes with him. She agrees, and tells him the honor of the day will not be his, for the LORD “will sell Sisera into a woman’s hand.”

The LORD confuses Sisera and his chariots at the river Kishon, and Sisera runs away on foot to the tent of Jael, whose husband’s family has peace with his king. She gives him milk and covers him with a rug. When he sleeps, she takes a tent peg and a hammer. Barak arrives to find Sisera already dead.

Deborah is the only judge described as a prophet, and the only one who settles disputes in the way the book’s title suggests. The war was fought in the Jezreel valley, where chariots were strong. Chapter 5 retells the same victory as a poem. Readers have long asked about Jael’s act of killing a guest after offering him shelter; the text reports it and the song praises her, and different readers have judged it differently. Compare Judges 5:24.

After the battle comes the song. Deborah and Barak sing, and the first thing they do is bless the LORD, for leaders who “took the lead in Israel” and a people who “offered themselves willingly”.

The song looks back to Sinai, when the earth shook at the LORD’s presence. It remembers empty roads and frightened travelers, and the day Deborah rose “a mother in Israel.” It names the tribes who came: Ephraim, Benjamin, Zebulun, Issachar, Naphtali. It also names those who stayed home among the sheepfolds and the ships, and it curses the town of Meroz for not helping.

The battle itself is told in a few lines: kings fought, the stars fought, the river Kishon swept them away. Jael is blessed above women. Then the camera swings to a window, where Sisera’s mother waits, asking why his chariot is so slow, and her ladies say he must be dividing the spoil. The song ends with a prayer, and the land rests forty years.

Many scholars regard this song as one of the oldest pieces of writing in the Bible, though dates are debated. It is poetry, so it speaks in images such as the stars fighting, and the details differ in places from the prose telling in chapter 4. Poems like this celebrated victories; compare Exodus 15. The scene with Sisera’s mother is often noticed for letting the reader see the enemy’s home with something close to sympathy. The next chapter begins another cycle.

For seven years the Midianites come every harvest. They arrive with their camels like locusts, destroy the crops and leave Israel with nothing, so the people hide in caves and mountain strongholds. Israel cries out, and a prophet reminds them who brought them out of Egypt.

Then the story finds a young man named Gideon beating out wheat in a wine press, to hide it. An angel of the LORD sits under an oak and says, “The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor!” Gideon answers with his questions: if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened? He says his family is the poorest in Manasseh, and he is the least in his father’s house. He asks for a sign, and fire comes up from a rock.

That night Gideon pulls down his father’s altar of Baal. He does it by night, because he is afraid, and the town wants him dead. Then, before the battle, he puts out a fleece, twice, and asks God for dew on the wool alone and then on the ground alone.

Midian and Amalek were desert peoples who raided from the east. The cycle begun in Judges 2 comes round again, and this time God’s first answer is a prophet’s rebuke, then a hesitant man. Gideon’s second name, Jerub-Baal, comes from his father’s defense of him. The fleece has been taken in different ways: some see it as a sign of faith, others as a sign of doubt. The text does not say which. Gideon’s call can be compared with Moses in Exodus 3.

Gideon rises early with an army. The LORD says it is too big: if Israel wins with all these men, they will brag that their own hand saved them. So the fearful are told to go home, and twenty-two thousand leave. Ten thousand remain, and the LORD says that is still too many.

At the water, those who lap like a dog are set apart from those who kneel, and only three hundred remain. That night the LORD tells Gideon, if you are afraid, go down to the enemy camp and listen. He hears a man tell a dream about a loaf of barley bread tumbling into the tent of Midian and flattening it. His friend says it can mean only Gideon’s sword. Gideon bows in worship.

He divides the three hundred into three companies, each man with a trumpet and a jar with a torch inside. At the edge of the camp they blow, break the jars and shout, “The sword of the LORD and of Gideon!” The Midianite army runs, and the men of Ephraim are called out to cut them off.

The point of the story is the shrinking army: the victory is meant to be the LORD’s. The battle is set in the valley of Jezreel, near the spring of Harod and the hill of Moreh. Trumpets, jars and torches are surprise weapons, used for panic and noise, and not for fighting. Compare the fall of Jericho in Joshua 6, where sound also played a part. Chapter 8 begins with the aftermath, which is less simple than the victory.

Victory does not end Gideon’s troubles. First the men of Ephraim rebuke him sharply for not calling them, and he calms them with a gentle answer about their share in the win. Then, faint but still pursuing, he and his three hundred ask the town of Succoth for bread. The leaders refuse, and so do the men of Penuel. Gideon promises both towns that he will come back, and he does. He catches the two Midianite kings, Zebah and Zalmunna, and punishes the elders of Succoth, and he breaks down the tower of Penuel and kills its men.

The kings are asked about the men they killed at Tabor, and Gideon says they were his brothers. He kills the kings himself.

The people then offer him a throne: “Rule over us”. He refuses: “The LORD shall rule over you.” But he asks for gold, and makes an ephod from it, and Israel goes after it. When he dies, they turn to the Baals again.

The chapter shows a hero with real strengths and real flaws. His answer to Ephraim shows wisdom, and his harshness toward Succoth and Penuel is hard to read. The ephod was a priestly garment, and here it becomes a snare; the text uses the language of unfaithfulness. Gideon’s refusal to be king is set against his son Abimelech in chapter 9. Compare the later request for a king in 1 Samuel 8.

Gideon had seventy sons, and one more by a concubine in Shechem: Abimelech. As soon as Gideon is gone, Abimelech goes to his mother’s family in Shechem and asks whether it is better to be ruled by seventy or by one. With silver from the temple of Baal Berith he hires reckless men, goes to his father’s house, and kills his brothers on one stone. Only the youngest, Jotham, hides.

When Shechem makes Abimelech king, Jotham climbs Mount Gerizim and tells a story about trees looking for a king. The olive, the fig and the vine all refuse. The bramble accepts. Jotham curses: let fire come out of Abimelech and devour Shechem, and out of Shechem and devour Abimelech.

Three years later the curse begins to come true. Shechem turns against Abimelech, and he destroys the city, burns a tower with about a thousand people inside, and then moves on to Thebez. There a woman drops a millstone on his head. He asks his armor bearer to kill him, so no one can say a woman did it.

This is the darkest chapter in the book. Abimelech is not a judge in the usual sense: he is a self-appointed king who seizes power by murder. Jotham’s fable is one of the oldest in the Bible, and it argues that those fit to rule do not want to. The text says God repaid the wickedness of both Abimelech and the men of Shechem. Shechem was an old center of worship and covenant; see Joshua 24. For another woman and a fatal blow, compare Judges 4.

After Abimelech, the book moves quickly through two quieter judges. Tola, from Issachar, judges twenty-three years. Jair of Gilead judges twenty-two, and has thirty sons who ride thirty donkey colts and rule thirty towns.

Then the old pattern returns. Israel serves the Baals and the Ashtaroth and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and the Philistines. The LORD gives them to the Philistines and the Ammonites, who crush Israel for eighteen years. Then the people cry out: “We have sinned against you”.

The LORD’s first answer is hard. He reminds them of the times he saved them and says: “Go and cry to the gods which you have chosen.” They plead again, “Do to us whatever seems good to you; only deliver us, please, today.” Then they put away the foreign gods. The text says the LORD’s soul was grieved for the misery of Israel. The Ammonites gather in Gilead, and the leaders ask who will lead the fight.

The chapter bridges the story of Abimelech and the story of Jephthah. It lists two judges in a few lines, and the contrast with the long accounts of Gideon and Abimelech is deliberate. The call for help is the same as in earlier cycles, but God’s reply is sharper, as the mood of the book darkens. Readers have taken the phrase about the LORD’s grief as a sign of his patience. Compare the prayer of repentance in 1 Samuel 7. Jephthah follows in chapter 11.

Jephthah is a mighty man of valor, and the son of a prostitute. His half brothers drive him out so he will not inherit, and outlaws gather around him in the land of Tob. When the Ammonites attack Gilead, the same elders who rejected him come to ask him to lead. He asks, “Didn’t you hate me”, and they promise to make him head over all.

He sends the Ammonite king a long message, arguing from Israel’s history that the land is not theirs. The king ignores it. The LORD’s Spirit comes on Jephthah, and he makes a vow: whatever comes out of his house to meet him when he returns in peace will be the LORD’s, and he will offer it as a burnt offering.

He wins a great victory. When he comes home, the first to come out is his daughter, his only child, dancing with tambourines. He tears his clothes. She says, “do to me according to that which has proceeded out of your mouth,” and asks for two months in the mountains. Then the text says her father did with her according to his vow.

This is one of the most painful stories in the Bible. The text says plainly what Jephthah vowed and what happened. Some readers and traditions understand that he sacrificed his daughter; others, including some ancient and medieval interpreters, read it as lifelong dedication to the LORD in a state of virginity. The law forbids human sacrifice; see Deuteronomy 12 and 18. The text never says the vow was right or that God asked for it.

The victory against Ammon is hardly over when Israel turns on itself. The men of Ephraim confront Jephthah, angry that they were not called, and threaten to burn his house down around him. Jephthah answers that he did call them and they did not come.

Then the Gileadites fight Ephraim and take the fords of the Jordan. Anyone who comes to the river and says “Let me go over” is asked if he is an Ephraimite. If he says no, they tell him to say Shibboleth. An Ephraimite says Sibboleth, because he cannot manage the sound, and he is killed there. The text counts forty-two thousand of Ephraim fallen.

Jephthah judges six years and dies. Three more judges are given a few lines each: Ibzan of Bethlehem with thirty sons and thirty daughters, Elon of Zebulun for ten years, and Abdon with forty sons and thirty grandsons on seventy donkey colts.

The quarrel between Ephraim and the tribes east of the Jordan echoes a similar conflict with Gideon in Judges 8, but here it turns to bloodshed. The story of the password gave the English language the word shibboleth, meaning a test of identity. It also shows a people who are fighting among themselves just when they should be united. The short notices about the minor judges show how little is told about most of them. Samson, the next judge, is introduced in chapter 13.

Israel is in the hands of the Philistines for forty years, and the story narrows to a childless couple in Zorah. Manoah’s wife is barren, and the LORD’s angel appears to her with news: “you shall conceive and bear a son.” He will be a Nazirite to God from the womb, so she must drink no wine and eat nothing unclean, and no razor will touch his head. He will begin to save Israel from the Philistines.

She tells her husband, and says the visitor looked very awesome. Manoah prays that the man of God will come again and teach them how to raise the child. The angel returns to the woman in the field, and she runs to bring her husband.

Manoah offers a young goat on a rock, and the angel goes up in the flame. The couple fall on their faces. Manoah says, “We shall surely die, because we have seen God.” His wife answers that if the LORD wanted to kill them, he would not have accepted their offering. A son is born. They name him Samson.

A Nazirite was a person set apart for a time by a vow, with rules about wine, hair and the dead; see Numbers 6. Samson is a Nazirite from birth, which is unusual. Stories of unexpected births appear throughout the Bible, such as Sarah in Genesis 18 and Hannah in 1 Samuel 1. The woman is not named here, but she appears as the wiser of the two. The angel’s name, called incomprehensible, echoes Genesis 32. The chapter opens the account of Samson that continues through chapter 16.

Samson goes down to Timnah and sees a Philistine woman. He comes home and tells his parents to get her for him. They ask whether there is no woman among their own people, but he answers, “Get her for me, for she pleases me well.” The text adds that his parents did not know the matter was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines.

On the road a young lion roars at him, and the LORD’s Spirit comes mightily on him. Later he finds bees and honey in the carcass and eats as he walks. At the wedding feast he sets thirty companions a riddle with clothing as the wager. For days they cannot answer, then they threaten his wife with fire. She weeps until he tells her, and she tells them. Samson goes to Ashkelon in anger, and his wife is given to his companion.

Judges tells of a time when the Philistines ruled over Israel and, in the book's own words elsewhere, everyone did what was right in their own eyes. Samson is one of the judges, a leader raised up in a crisis. This chapter opens his story as a marriage that goes wrong. Samson's Nazirite background is told earlier in the book (see Judges 13). Readers differ on how to weigh Samson: some see a flawed man God still used, others stress how the book shows a people and a leader far from God's ways.

Samson comes back at wheat harvest with a young goat, hoping to see his wife. Her father will not let him in. He had thought Samson hated her, so he gave her to Samson’s companion, and he offers her younger sister instead. Samson answers that this time he will be blameless when he harms the Philistines.

He catches three hundred foxes, ties them tail to tail with torches, and sends them into the standing grain and the olive groves. The Philistines burn his wife and her father. Samson takes revenge and hides in a cave at Etam.

Then the Philistines camp in Judah, and three thousand men of Judah come to bind Samson and hand him over. He lets them. At Lehi the ropes fall from his arms, and with a fresh jawbone of a donkey he strikes a thousand men. Thirsty, he calls on the LORD, and God opens water from a hollow place.

This chapter continues the cycle of revenge that began at the wedding in Judges 14. It also shows Israel's condition under the Philistines: the men of Judah are not rising to fight but are ready to give Samson up to keep the peace. The writer notes that Samson judged Israel twenty years. The chapter is violent, and the text itself shows harm passing from person to person. Christians read Samson's prayer for water as a sign that his strength is not his own.

Samson goes to Gaza, and the men of the city wait at the gate all night to kill him at morning light. At midnight he pulls up the gate doors, posts and bar, and carries them to a hilltop before Hebron.

Then he loves a woman named Delilah. The Philistine lords each offer her eleven hundred pieces of silver to learn the secret of his strength. Three times he lies, and three times she cries, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” At last, pressed daily, his soul is troubled to death, and he tells her all: he has been a Nazirite to God from birth, and no razor has touched his head.

She has him shaved. He wakes and does not know that the LORD has left him. The Philistines put out his eyes and set him to grind at the mill. At a feast to Dagon he is called out to entertain them. He prays once more and pulls down the pillars.

Samson's story ends here, at the low point of the book's second half. A Nazirite, set apart to God, had a vow that included leaving the hair uncut (see Numbers 6). The text names the loss of his hair and the LORD's departure together. The Philistines credit their god Dagon with the victory. Christians read Samson's last prayer in different ways: as a flawed man's final trust in God, or as a sign of how far the judges era had fallen. The text says he judged Israel twenty years.

A man named Micah, from the hill country of Ephraim, confesses to his mother that he took her eleven hundred pieces of silver, the money she had cursed the thief over. She answers by blessing him in the LORD’s name. He gives the silver back, and she dedicates it to the LORD to make a carved image and a molten image.

So a house of gods stands in Micah’s home, with an ephod, household idols, and one of his sons as priest. Then the book states the problem in two short sentences: there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes.

A young Levite from Bethlehem, looking for a place to live, comes to the door. Micah hires him as a father and priest for ten pieces of silver a year, clothing and food. Micah is satisfied. Now, he says, he knows the LORD will do him good.

With this chapter the book of Judges moves from the stories of the judges to two accounts that show Israel's condition without a leader (Judges 17 to 21). The refrain about no king is repeated here and at the end of the book. Many scholars think it hints at a time before the monarchy and perhaps at an argument for it. The chapter mixes the LORD's name with images and idols, which the law forbids (see Exodus 20). The Levite's story continues in Judges 18.

The tribe of Dan has not yet settled its inheritance, so it sends five men to spy out the land. They lodge at Micah’s house, recognize the young Levite’s voice, and ask what he is doing there. When they ask for a word from God, he tells them “Go in peace”.

At Laish they find a quiet people living in safety, far from help. They report that God has given the land into their hand. Six hundred armed Danites set out, and the five point them to the images in Micah’s house.

They take the images and offer the priest a larger post: priest to a tribe instead of one man’s house. His heart is glad. Micah chases them, sees they are too strong, and turns back. The Danites strike Laish with the sword, burn it, and rename it Dan. They set up the image, with Jonathan, a grandson of Moses by the text’s account, and his sons as priests.

This chapter follows the Levite and the images from Judges 17. The refrain returns that there was no king in Israel. The book shows a tribe taking by force a land that was quiet and far from help, and building a worship around a stolen idol. The chapter ends by noting that the image stood all the time God's house was at Shiloh. Readers often see this as the book's way of marking how far worship had wandered from what the law set out.

A Levite from the far side of the hill country of Ephraim takes a concubine from Bethlehem. She leaves him for her father’s house, and after four months he goes to bring her back, speaking kindly to her. Her father welcomes him and keeps him for days.

When the man finally leaves late in the day, he refuses to lodge in Jebus, a foreign city, and goes on to Gibeah in Benjamin. No one takes them in until an old man coming home from the fields offers shelter.

That night the men of the city surround the house and demand the guest. The old man offers his own daughter and the concubine instead. The Levite pushes his concubine out to them, and they abuse her all night. In the morning she lies at the door with her hands on the threshold. She does not answer when he tells her to get up. At home he cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them through all Israel.

This is among the hardest chapters of the Bible. The book describes a brutal crime and does not excuse it. It stands in the final section of Judges (see Judges 17 to 21), where the refrain that there was no king in Israel frames the story. Readers note the echo of the men of Sodom in Genesis 19. The text says what happened to the woman and says it is not to be forgotten: those who see the pieces say such a deed has not been done since Israel left Egypt. The story is not offered as a model to follow.

All Israel gathers at Mizpah as one man, four hundred thousand who draw the sword. The Levite tells them what happened at Gibeah. They vow that none will go home until Gibeah is dealt with. They ask Benjamin to hand over the guilty men, but Benjamin will not listen and gathers for war.

Israel goes up to Bethel and asks God who should go first. The LORD says Judah. On the first day Benjamin destroys twenty-two thousand Israelites, and on the second day eighteen thousand. Israel weeps, fasts, and offers sacrifices. This time the answer is “Go up; for tomorrow I will deliver him into your hand”.

On the third day Israel pretends to retreat and draws Benjamin away while an ambush takes the city. A column of smoke is the signal. Benjamin looks back and sees the city going up in smoke. Twenty-five thousand one hundred Benjamites fall. Only six hundred escape to the rock of Rimmon.

This chapter follows the crime at Gibeah in Judges 19. The tribes act together, which they have not done in much of the book. Yet the story ends with a tribe almost wiped out. The text is open about Israel's losses: they lose forty thousand men before they win. They ask God and are answered, but the war ends in near destruction of a brother tribe. Readers differ on whether the book approves of the war or shows its tragedy. The conclusion in Judges 21 deals with the survivors.

After the war, Israel weeps. They had sworn at Mizpah not to give their daughters to Benjamin, and now a tribe is nearly gone. They sit before God at Bethel until evening and ask why one tribe should be lacking in Israel today.

They look for a way to keep their oath and still find wives for the six hundred men. No one from Jabesh Gilead had come to Mizpah, so twelve thousand men destroy that city, sparing four hundred young women, who are given to Benjamin. It is not enough.

So the elders tell the Benjamites to hide in the vineyards at the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh and carry off wives from the dancing daughters. The men do so and rebuild their cities. The book closes where Judges 17 began: there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes.

This is the end of Judges. The Israelites grieve for Benjamin as a brother, yet their solution adds new violence and takes women without their consent. The text records these acts and does not praise them. The closing refrain about no king, and about everyone doing what was right in their own eyes, sums up the book's last chapters (see Judges 17 to 21). Many scholars read it as preparing for the books of Samuel, where Israel gets a king. The next book in this Bible is Ruth.
